title: Phulkari, stitched flowers
hookLine: Punjab's flower-embroidered shawls, made by women and given at weddings

lines: A TRUNK OPENED ON A WEDDING MORNING.
cards: A wedding morning in a Punjabi home. The bride sits very still while her mother lifts a heavy shawl out of a trunk and unfolds it over her shoulders. The cloth underneath is rough, hand-spun cotton, a deep red.
But you can barely see it. Almost every inch is covered in silk thread, golden and orange and white, laid down in tiny straight stitches that catch the light and turn it into a field of flowers.
Someone in the family made this, slowly, over a long time, for this morning. Today's word is that shawl.

teach.b: First, what it is. Phul is the Punjabi word for flower, and a phulkari is flower work: a shawl or head cloth embroidered in bright silk floss on hand-spun cotton.
When the stitching covers the whole cloth, so the cotton disappears beneath it, people call it a bagh, a garden. Second, how it's made.

teach.h: WORKED FROM THE BACK, BY COUNT.
teach.b: Phulkari is worked largely from the back of the cloth, counting threads, in long darning stitches that lie flat and shine on the front. For some designs no pattern is drawn; it lives in the maker's head and hands.
That's slow work, done in the gaps of a day, often with other women sitting close, talking. Third, what it carries. Phulkari belongs to Punjab's women across faiths, Sikh, Hindu and Muslim.
Tradition in some families says a grandmother starts a bagh when a granddaughter is born, to give at her wedding.
Whether or not a family keeps that custom, the shawl comes out at the big moments: weddings, births, celebrations. Fourth, why it sits in this path. In the Asa di Var, Guru Nanak speaks up for women.
In paraphrase: why call her lesser, she from whom kings are born?

A phulkari is women's work and women's wisdom, made by hand and handed down. It honors the ones who made it, the ones who wear it, and the long line between them: a story told without words, stitch by stitch.

how: Phulkari shawls and baghs are embroidered by Punjabi women and brought out for weddings, births and celebrations; some families keep old ones as heirlooms, and the craft is still taught.

games.q: you're starting a phulkari for a granddaughter's wedding, and there's no pattern drawn on the cloth. what do you do?
o: wait until someone draws a pattern.
work from the back, counting threads, with the pattern in your head.
games.why: phulkari is worked largely from the back, by count, and for some designs the pattern lives in the maker's head and hands.

practice: If there's stitched cloth near you, a cushion, a scarf, a hem, look at it close up and follow one thread with your eyes, noticing how many tiny decisions sit in a single flower.
If nothing is near, think of something made by hand for you by someone who took their time, and stay with that patience a while.

wordCard.voice: Phulkari. Flower work: Punjab's shawls embroidered in bright silk on hand-spun cotton, made by women and given at weddings and births. Today's word.
